description: SarASight aims to make Earth’s changes visible and understandable. For “Dancing with the SARs,” we plan to use NISAR radar data to explore flood-related surface changes through interactive maps, before-and-after comparisons, and clear explanations. Our goal is to support disaster-impact assessment with local relevance to Pakistan and potential worldwide applications. Our approach will evolve during the hackathon based on available data.
summary:
FloodLens turns radar images of the 2022 Upper Sindh floods into something relief teams can act on and check. Floods hide under monsoon cloud, but radar sees through cloud and night. Using Sentinel-1 radar from the same orbit on 18 and 30 August 2022, we map the flood across Dadu, Larkana and Kamber Shahdadkot. We then count what it reached: about 7,900 km² of flood, roughly 3 million people living inside flooded pixels, and over 5,400 km² of cropland. We also show NASA-ISRO’s new NISAR L-band radar over Dadu in 2026, next to Sentinel-1.

A LightGBM model gives a second opinion on the physics-based map, and SHAP shows why each pixel is called flood. Every input and output carries a SHA-256 fingerprint, and an orbit audit confirms the images match, so anyone can check that nothing changed.

We state our limits openly. No ground truth exists for Sindh 2022, so we claim no accuracy there. The model was tested only on a held-out event, Pakistan 2017, and its precision is low, so we treat its map as an upper bound.
details:
The story

In August 2022, floods covered a large part of Upper Sindh, Pakistan. The monsoon sky was full of cloud, so normal satellite photos could not see the water. Radar can see through cloud and night, but raw radar data is hard to read, and even a clean flood map leaves relief teams with two questions: how many people and how much farmland were hit, and can we trust this map? FloodLens was built to answer both.

How it works

We start with Sentinel-1 radar over Dadu, Larkana and Kamber Shahdadkot, using images from the same orbit and flight direction on 18 and 30 August 2022, so both views look at the ground from the same angle. Calm water is smooth, so it looks dark in radar. We flag pixels that are very dark and also became darker between the two dates, then clean the result. Permanent rivers (JRC Surface Water), steep slopes that mimic water (Copernicus DEM) and radar noise are removed.

Next, we turn the map into impact numbers using WorldPop and ESA WorldCover. Our main map shows about 7,900 km² of flood, roughly 3 million people living inside flooded pixels and about 5,500 km² of cropland.

Science and explainability

A LightGBM model, trained on the Sen1Floods11 hand-labelled flood dataset, gives a second opinion. We tested it on Pakistan 2017, a flood it never saw. Precision is low (0.17), so we treat its map as an upper bound, and the area where both methods agree as the careful estimate. SHAP shows why each pixel is called flood. VH radar backscatter matters most, which matches the physics.

Trust and data integrity

Every input and output carries a SHA-256 fingerprint, and an audit confirms both scenes share the same orbit. Anyone can check that nothing changed. We also show NASA-ISRO’s new NISAR L-band radar over Dadu in 2026 (provisional data) next to Sentinel-1. It is not a view of the 2022 flood.

Benefits and impact

Relief planners, district authorities and researchers get a quick first look: where the water went, who and what it reached, and how far to trust it. The method can be re-run for a new flood once a Sentinel-1 stack is prepared.

Tools
Tools: Python, Google Earth Engine (Sentinel-1 radar from ESA Copernicus), NASA Earthdata and the ASF DAAC (NISAR L-band radar), rasterio, h5py, LightGBM, SHAP, scikit-learn, pandas, Plotly, Folium and Streamlit. We worked on standard laptops, with no special hardware. We used Claude as an AI assistant for coding and writing support. The team ran the data processing and reviewed all results.

What is creative

Our idea is not a new flood map. It is a flood map you can check: decision-ready numbers, explanation, proof of integrity and openly stated limits, in one web app.

Limits we considered

No ground truth exists for Sindh 2022, so we claim no accuracy there. Flood extent is the water seen when the satellite passed. Dry sandy ground can look dark and inflate the area. Roads and hospitals are planned next.
